---
title: "Coding assistants in the terminal"
subtitle: "An optional introduction: install one agent, give it a real task, and check its work"
---

A *coding assistant* (or coding agent) is a language model that runs in a loop on your machine: it reads files, proposes edits, runs commands such as your tests, reads the output, and decides its next step. The four on this page all work from the terminal. They are a practical example of the agents you build in [Module 14](lectures/14-agents.qmd): a model, a set of tools, and a permission policy that decides which tool calls need your approval.

None of them is required for the workshop. The labs run in Colab without any of them.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Install commands and flags were checked on {{< var assistants.checked >}} against Codex {{< var assistants.codex >}}, Claude Code {{< var assistants.claude_code >}}, Gemini CLI {{< var assistants.gemini_cli >}} and Kimi Code {{< var assistants.kimi_code >}}. These tools change every week. If a command fails, check the tool's own documentation, linked in each tab.
:::

## The four tools at a glance

| | Codex | Claude Code | Gemini CLI | Kimi Code |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Made by | OpenAI | Anthropic | Google | Moonshot AI |
| Command | `codex` | `claude` | `gemini` | `kimi` |
| Account | ChatGPT plan or OpenAI API key | Claude Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise or Console | Google account (free tier) or Gemini API key | Kimi account or Moonshot API key |
| Project instructions file | `AGENTS.md` | `CLAUDE.md`, or `AGENTS.md` if there is no `CLAUDE.md` | `GEMINI.md` | `AGENTS.md` |
| One-shot (headless) mode | `codex exec` | `claude -p` | `gemini -p` | `kimi -p` |

A *project instructions file* is a Markdown file at the root of a repository that the agent reads at the start of every session: build commands, conventions, what not to touch. This repository's own [`AGENTS.md`]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/AGENTS.md) is an example.

## Before you start

- **A terminal on macOS, Linux or Windows.** On Windows, use PowerShell; WSL also works.
- **Python 3.10 or later and `pytest`** for the task below: `python3 -m pip install pytest`.
- **Node.js** only if you install with `npm`. Each tab gives the version it needs.
- **Read what the agent does.** Every tool asks before it runs a command unless you tell it not to. Approve commands you understand; decline the rest.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
An agent sends the files it reads to its provider. Do not run one in a folder that holds secrets, such as a `.env` file with API keys. Avoid the flags that skip all approvals (`--yolo`, `--auto`, `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`) except inside a container or a throwaway virtual machine.
:::

## The task

The same task works in every tab, so you can compare the tools. It rebuilds a piece of [Module 1](lectures/01-text-as-data.qmd), an n-gram language model scored by perplexity, and it asks the agent to test its own work.

Create an empty project with the Tiny Shakespeare text, the same file the labs use:

```bash
mkdir bigram-demo && cd bigram-demo
git init -q
curl -fsSL -o input.txt {{< var datasets.fallback_base >}}/tinyshakespeare.txt
```

Save this prompt as `TASK.md` in the same folder:

```text
Build a character-level bigram language model with add-k smoothing in bigram.py.
Use the characters of the whole of input.txt as the vocabulary. Train on the first
90% of input.txt and print the perplexity on the last 10% for k = 0.01, 0.1 and 1.

Write tests in test_bigram.py that check:
1. for every context character, the next-character probabilities sum to 1;
2. a bigram never seen in training gets a probability above zero;
3. perplexity on the training text is lower than on the held-out text.

Use only the Python standard library and pytest. Run the tests and fix any
failure before you finish. Then summarise what you built in three lines.
```

Then open the tab for your tool. Each one installs the tool, signs you in, and runs the task. The last step in each tab, a code review, is for one of your own repositories with work on a branch: the demo folder has no branch to compare against.

::: {.panel-tabset group="assistant"}

## Codex

**Install** (needs Node.js 16 or later for npm):

```bash
npm install -g @openai/codex        # macOS, Linux, Windows
brew install --cask codex           # macOS, with Homebrew
codex --version
```

**Sign in.** Run `codex` and choose *Sign in with ChatGPT* (Plus, Pro, Business, Edu or Enterprise plans). To use an API key instead:

```bash
printenv OPENAI_API_KEY | codex login --with-api-key
```

**Run the task.** Start Codex in the project folder with a sandbox that lets it write only inside that folder, and let it ask before anything else:

```bash
codex --sandbox workspace-write --ask-for-approval on-request "$(cat TASK.md)"
```

The same task without the interactive screen, with the final answer saved to a file:

```bash
codex exec --sandbox workspace-write -o summary.md "$(cat TASK.md)"
```

**Review a branch.** Codex has a built-in reviewer. In one of your own repositories, review the changes you have not committed yet, or the current branch against `main`:

```bash
codex review --uncommitted
codex review --base main
```

**Project instructions:** `AGENTS.md`. Documentation: [developers.openai.com/codex](https://developers.openai.com/codex) and [github.com/openai/codex](https://github.com/openai/codex).

## Claude Code

**Install.** The native installer needs no Node.js and updates itself:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash      # macOS, Linux, WSL
```

```powershell
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex             # Windows PowerShell
```

Alternatives: `brew install --cask claude-code` (macOS), `winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode` (Windows), or `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code` (Node.js 22 or later). Then check the install:

```bash
claude --version
claude doctor
```

**Sign in.** Run `claude` and follow the browser prompt. It needs a Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise or Console account; the free Claude plan does not include Claude Code. If `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is set, Claude Code asks once whether to use that key instead.

**Run the task.** Start Claude Code in the project folder. `acceptEdits` lets it write files without asking; it still asks before running commands such as `pytest`:

```bash
claude --permission-mode acceptEdits "$(cat TASK.md)"
```

The same task without the interactive screen. In `-p` mode nobody can answer a prompt, so you list the commands it may run:

```bash
claude -p "$(cat TASK.md)" --permission-mode acceptEdits \
  --allowedTools "Bash(python *),Bash(python3 *),Bash(pytest *)"
```

**Review a branch.** In one of your own repositories, pipe the branch's diff in. Claude reads it from standard input, so it needs no permission to run `git`:

```bash
git diff main | claude -p "Review this diff for bugs and missing tests. Cite file:line."
```

**Project instructions:** `CLAUDE.md`, or the repository's `AGENTS.md` when there is no `CLAUDE.md`. Documentation: [code.claude.com/docs](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/setup).

## Gemini CLI

**Install** (needs Node.js 20 or later):

```bash
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli   # macOS, Linux, Windows
brew install gemini-cli             # macOS or Linux, with Homebrew
gemini --version
```

To try it without installing anything: `npx @google/gemini-cli`.

**Sign in.** Run `gemini` and choose *Sign in with Google*. A personal Google account gets a free tier of 60 requests a minute and 1,000 a day. To use an API key from Google AI Studio instead:

```bash
export GEMINI_API_KEY="your-key"
```

**Run the task.** Start Gemini CLI with the task as its first prompt and stay in the session. `auto_edit` approves file edits and still asks before shell commands:

```bash
gemini --approval-mode auto_edit -i "$(cat TASK.md)"
```

Use `--approval-mode plan` for a read-only session in which Gemini can read and plan but not change anything.

**Review a branch.** In one of your own repositories, pipe the branch's diff in. In headless mode (`-p`), Gemini appends the prompt to whatever arrives on standard input:

```bash
git diff main | gemini -p "Review this diff for bugs and missing tests. Cite file:line."
```

Add `--output-format json` when a script will read the answer.

**Project instructions:** `GEMINI.md`. Documentation: [github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli).

## Kimi Code

Kimi Code replaces Moonshot AI's earlier Python tool, `kimi-cli`, which is archived. Install the new one.

**Install.** The install script verifies a checksum and puts `kimi` on your `PATH`:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://code.kimi.com/kimi-code/install.sh | bash   # macOS, Linux
```

```powershell
irm https://code.kimi.com/kimi-code/install.ps1 | iex          # Windows PowerShell
```

Alternatives: `brew install kimi-code`, or `npm install -g @moonshot-ai/kimi-code` (Node.js 22.19 or later). On Windows, Kimi Code also needs [Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/downloads/win) for its shell. Then check the install:

```bash
kimi --version
kimi doctor
```

**Sign in.** Run `kimi login` for a device-code sign-in in the browser (add `--region global` for kimi.ai accounts or `--region mainland-cn` for kimi.com). Inside a session, `/login` also accepts a Moonshot API key.

**Run the task.** Kimi Code has no argument for a first prompt, so start it and paste the contents of `TASK.md`:

```bash
kimi
```

By default it asks before edits and commands. `kimi --plan` starts in plan mode, where it proposes a plan before it changes anything. `kimi --yolo` runs routine edits and commands without asking but still asks before risky actions.

`kimi -p "…"` runs one prompt without the interactive screen and prints the answer. We have not checked how it handles an action that needs approval, so use it below only for a prompt that needs no tools.

**Review a branch.** In one of your own repositories, pass the branch's diff inside the prompt:

```bash
kimi -p "Review this diff for bugs and missing tests. Cite file:line.
$(git diff main)"
```

**Project instructions:** `AGENTS.md`. Documentation: [github.com/MoonshotAI/kimi-code](https://github.com/MoonshotAI/kimi-code).

:::

## Check the agent's work

An agent's summary says what it meant to do, not what it did. Check the result yourself:

```bash
python3 -m pytest -q          # all three tests should pass
python3 bigram.py             # held-out perplexity for each k
git status && git diff        # every file the agent changed
```

What to expect. The text has 65 distinct characters, so a model that guesses uniformly has a perplexity of 65. A bigram model should reach about 12 on the held-out 10%, nearly the same for all three values of `k`. Our own reference solution gives 12.03, 11.99 and 11.96 for k = 0.01, 0.1 and 1. A number above 65 or below 1 means a bug. So do tests that pass only because they test nothing: open `test_bigram.py` and read each assertion.

Then try one follow-up in the same session, and check it the same way:

- *"Add a trigram model and compare its held-out perplexity with the bigram's."*
- *"Make test 1 fail on purpose by breaking the smoothing, show me the failure, then restore it."*

## How these tools relate to the workshop

| On this page | In the workshop |
|---|---|
| Model, tools and a loop that reads tool output | The hand-written tool loop in [Module 8](lectures/08-llm-apis.qmd) |
| Approval modes, sandboxes, allowed-tool lists | The tool guard and human-in-the-loop interrupts in [Module 14](lectures/14-agents.qmd) |
| "Fix any failure before you finish" | Evaluation against a fixed check, as in [Module 13](lectures/13-rag.qmd) and the [capstone](lectures/15-capstone.qmd) |
| Add-k smoothing, the sum-to-one test, perplexity | The same equations and checkpoint in [Module 1](lectures/01-text-as-data.qmd) |
